s1.q: A problem says n can be up to 100,000 and your time limit is about one second. Which running time is realistic?
s1.why: n² = 10¹⁰ operations is far above the ~10⁸ budget. n log n ≈ 1.7 million is comfortable.

s1.q: Which clue most strongly suggests backtracking?
o: "Find the shortest path in an unweighted graph"
"List every valid way to place 8 queens"
"Find the 5 largest values in a stream"
s1.why: "List every valid arrangement" means complete search with constraints. Shortest path is BFS, top-k is a heap, sorted insertion is a BST.

s1.q: Is the recursive factorial function a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
o: Yes, it has a base case
Yes, it splits n into n−1 and 1
No, it shrinks by a constant (n−1), not by a fraction of the input
No, because it is not recursive
s1.why: Divide and conquer splits the input into fractions (like n/2). Factorial just peels off one element at a time.

s1.q: What is the space complexity of recursive factorial(n)?
s1.why: n frames are on the call stack at the deepest point.

s1.q: You wrote a solution and want to catch off-by-one errors. What is the most effective step?
o: Dry run on edge cases: empty, one element, duplicates
s1.why: Tracing small and extreme inputs by hand exposes boundary mistakes quickly.

s2.q: For f(n) = 3n² + 10n + 5, which statement is correct?
s2.why: f is both O(n²) (c=4, n₀=11) and Ω(n²) (c=3, n₀=1), so Θ(n²). It is O(n³) too, but not Θ(n³).

s2.q: What is the complexity of: i = 1; while i < n: i *= 2 ?
s2.why: i doubles each time, reaching n after log₂n steps.

s2.q: for i in range(n): for j in range(i): work() runs work() how many times?
T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n². What does the Master theorem give?
s2.why: a=9, b=3, so n^c = n². f(n) = n² equals it: Case 2, giving n² log n.

s2.q: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n. Which is true?
o: The basic Master theorem does not apply (gap case)
s2.why: n log n is larger than n but not polynomially larger (log n < n^ε). Recursion tree gives Θ(n log² n).

s2.q: The best-case running time of linear search is:
s2.why: The target is in the first position: one comparison.

s2.q: Which statement about Big-O and worst case is right?
o: Big-O is a kind of bound on a function; worst case is a choice of input. They are different ideas
Big-O is only for best case
Θ can only describe worst case
s2.why: You can give O, Ω or Θ bounds for the best, average or worst case separately.

s2.q: You loop over array a (n items) and, inside, over array b (m items). The cost is:
s2.why: Two different inputs stay as two variables: n × m iterations.

s3.q: With the last element as pivot, which input makes Quick Sort run in O(n²)?
s3.why: On sorted input, the last element is the maximum, so partition gives 0 and n−1 each time.

s3.q: After one call to partition, the pivot is:
s3.why: Everything left of it is ≤ it and everything right of it is bigger, so it is exactly where it belongs.

s3.q: A 1:9 split at every level gives:
s3.why: Any constant-proportion split keeps the depth O(log n) and each level costs O(n).

s3.q: Average-case extra space of Quick Sort is:
s3.why: Partition is in place; only the recursion stack uses memory, about log n deep on average.

s3.q: In Lomuto partition, what does k represent?
o: The index of the last element in the "≤ pivot" zone
s3.why: k starts at lo−1 and grows each time an element ≤ pivot is found. The pivot ends at k+1.

o: No, swaps can reorder equal elements
s3.why: Merge Sort is stable; the long-distance swaps in partition break stability.

s3.q: An array of n equal values is sorted with Lomuto partition (≤ pivot, last element pivot). The time is:
s3.why: Every element is ≤ pivot, so k runs to hi−1 and the split is n−1 : 0 every time.

s3.q: Which sorting facts are correct? Merge sort is ___, Quick Sort is ___.
o: stable and in-place; unstable and not in-place
stable but needs O(n) extra space; unstable but in place
s3.why: Merge sort is stable with an O(n) merge buffer. Quick Sort partitions in place but its swaps can reorder equal keys.

s3.q: No comparison sort can beat what worst-case bound?
s3.why: n! orderings need at least log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n) binary comparisons to tell apart.

s4.q: Which traversal of a BST outputs keys in sorted order?
s4.why: Inorder visits left, node, right, matching the BST ordering.

s4.q: Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (in that order) into an empty plain BST gives a tree of height:
s4.why: Every key goes to the right of the previous one: a chain of 5 nodes has height 4 (edges).

s4.q: To delete a node with two children, replace it with:
o: Its inorder successor (minimum of the right subtree)
s4.why: The successor is the smallest key bigger than the deleted one, so the BST rule survives. The predecessor also works.

s4.q: What is wrong with checking only "left child < node < right child" to validate a BST?
o: It ignores that every node in a subtree must respect all ancestors
It only works for balanced trees
s4.why: Root 10, left child 5, and 5's right child 15 passes the local check but 15 is in the left subtree of 10.

o: O(h), where h is the height
s4.why: One path from the root. h ≈ log n if balanced and n if skewed.

s4.q: You insert 5, 3, 8, 1, 4. What is the inorder traversal?
s4.why: Inorder of a BST is sorted: 1 3 4 5 8.

s4.q: Which traversal would you use to copy a tree (create the parent before its children)?
s4.why: Preorder visits the node first, so a parent is created before its children.

s4.q: A binary tree with 15 nodes has how many edges?
s4.why: Every node except the root has exactly one edge to its parent: n − 1.

s4.q: What is the maximum number of nodes on level 3 of a binary tree (root = level 0)?
s4.why: 2³ = 8: each level can at most double.

s4.q: A full binary tree has 7 internal nodes. How many leaves does it have?
s4.why: In a full binary tree, leaves = internal nodes + 1.

s4.q: "Everything in the left subtree is smaller, everything in the right subtree is larger" describes:
s4.why: That is the BST rule. A max-heap compares only parent with children (parent ≥ child).

Building a heap from n unsorted values using the bottom-up method takes:
s5.why: Most nodes are near the leaves and sift only a short distance; the sum of heights is O(n).

s5.q: When deleting the max from a max-heap, you swap the new root with its:
s5.why: Swapping with the larger child keeps the new parent ≥ both children.

s5.q: Which operation is slow in a heap?
s5.why: Siblings are unordered, so a search may have to look at every node: O(n).

s5.q: To find the k-th largest of n numbers in O(n log k), you keep:
o: A max-heap of all n items
s5.why: The min-heap holds the k largest seen so far; its top is the k-th largest.

s5.q: Inserting into a heap of n items takes at most how many swaps?
s5.why: The new node climbs one level per swap; the height is about log₂ n.

s5.q: Which of these is a valid max-heap array?
s5.why: Only [20, 10, 5] has the root ≥ both children.

s5.q: Which array is NOT a valid max-heap?
s5.why: In [9,5,8,6,2,3,7], index 3 (value 6) is a child of index 1 (value 5), and 6 > 5.

s5.q: A heap has 10 nodes (indices 0 to 9). Which indices are leaves?
s5.why: Leaves start at index n//2 = 5. The last parent is index (9−1)//2 = 4.

s5.q: Which statement about a max-heap is TRUE?
o: The left child is always smaller than the right child
Its array is sorted in decreasing order
The root is the largest, but siblings are not ordered
Searching for any value is O(log n)
s5.why: The heap only orders parents against children; siblings and search are unordered.

s6.q: What are the three steps repeated at every position in backtracking?
s6.why: Make a choice, recurse, then remove the choice before trying the next one.

s6.q: How many permutations of n distinct items are there?
s6.why: n choices for the first slot, n−1 for the second, and so on.

o: Skipping a branch as soon as it can no longer lead to a valid solution
s6.why: The whole subtree of a rejected choice is never explored.

s6.q: In N-Queens (row by row), why do we only check rows above the current one?
o: Rows below are still empty at that time
It is an optimisation that changes the answer
s6.why: We fill from the top, so only rows 0 .. row−1 can hold queens.

s6.q: How many solutions does the 4-Queens problem have?
s6.why: There are exactly two: columns (1,3,0,2) and (2,0,3,1).

s6.q: You store a result with res.append(cur) and later cur.pop() runs. What happens?
o: The stored result changes too, because it is the same list
s6.why: Lists are references. Save a copy: res.append(cur[:]).

s6.q: The number of subsets of an n-element set, which backtracking enumerates, is:
s6.why: Each element is either included or excluded.

s6.q: In the "design recipe" for backtracking, which question defines the base case?
s6.why: The base case is the moment the partial solution is a complete solution.

s7.q: In an undirected graph with 7 edges, the sum of all vertex degrees is:
s7.why: Each edge adds 1 to two vertices: 2E = 14.

s7.q: Space used by an adjacency matrix for V vertices:
s7.why: A V × V table, regardless of how many edges exist.

s7.q: Which representation is best for a sparse graph with 100,000 vertices?
s7.why: The list needs O(V + E); the matrix would need 10¹⁰ cells.

s7.q: The adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is:
s7.why: An undirected edge i–j sets both [i][j] and [j][i].

s7.q: Time to test whether an edge u–v exists in an adjacency list?
s7.why: You scan u's neighbour list. A matrix does it in O(1).

s7.q: In a directed graph, the sum of all in-degrees equals:
s7.why: Each edge contributes exactly one to some vertex's in-degree (and one to an out-degree).

s7.q: What makes a tree different from a general graph?
o: A tree is connected and has no cycles
s7.why: A tree is a connected acyclic graph, with exactly V − 1 edges.

s8.why: FIFO order discovers vertices level by level.

s8.q: BFS gives the shortest path in which kind of graph?
s8.why: BFS minimises the number of edges. Weighted graphs need Dijkstra.

s8.q: When should BFS mark a vertex as visited?
s8.why: Marking at enqueue prevents the same vertex being queued twice.

s8.q: Time complexity of DFS using adjacency lists:
s8.why: Every vertex is entered once and every edge is examined once or twice.

s8.q: In a directed graph, DFS finds a back edge. This means:
s8.why: A back edge points to an ancestor still on the stack, closing a cycle.

s8.q: How do you count connected components in an undirected graph?
o: Start a new DFS/BFS from each unvisited vertex and count the starts
s8.why: Each fresh start reaches exactly one new component.

s8.q: Rotting oranges uses multi-source BFS because:
o: There is more than one rotten orange at time 0, all spreading simultaneously
DFS cannot be used on grids
s8.why: Putting all rotten oranges in the queue at the start makes each BFS level equal to one minute.

s8.q: DFS on an adjacency matrix has time:
s8.why: Finding the neighbours of each vertex scans a whole row of length V.

s9.q: Which pair of properties must a problem have for DP to apply?
s9.why: Overlapping subproblems make caching worthwhile; optimal substructure lets us build the answer from sub-answers.

s9.q: Climbing stairs (steps of 1 or 2): the recurrence is
s9.why: The last move is either a 1-step from i−1 or a 2-step from i−2; the ways add.

s9.q: Time complexity of the naive recursive climbing stairs?
s9.why: Each call makes two more calls and subproblems repeat enormously.

s9.q: Memoized climbing stairs has time complexity:
s9.why: Each of the n+1 distinct subproblems is computed once, in O(1) work.
Either skip house i (keep dp[i−1]) or rob it (add to dp[i−2]).

To reduce the space of House Robber to O(1) you keep:

s9.q: Which is NOT a feature of memoization?
o: Fills a table with loops from the smallest case
s9.why: Filling a table with loops from small to large is tabulation (bottom-up).

o: Serve items in the order they arrived
Remove the most recently added item first
s0.why: LIFO: last in, first out, like a pile of plates.

s0.q: Which structure should BFS use for its to-do list?
s0.why: A queue serves vertices in the order they were discovered, giving level-by-level order.

s0.q: About how many times can 1,000,000 be halved before reaching 1?
Why use collections.deque instead of a list for a queue?
o: list.pop(0) is O(n) but deque.popleft() is O(1)
s0.why: Removing from the front of a list shifts every other element.

s0.q: In a linked list, reaching the i-th item costs:
o: O(i), following pointers one at a time
s0.why: There is no index arithmetic; you must follow next pointers.

s10.q: LCS of strings of length m and n: how big is the DP table?
s10.why: There is an extra row and column for the empty prefix, which is the base case (all zeros).

s10.q: In LCS, when the last letters xᵢ and yⱼ are different, c[i][j] equals:
s10.why: They cannot both end the common subsequence, so drop one of them and keep the better result.

s10.q: Running time of the LCS dynamic program:

o: dp[i][c] = max(dp[i−1][c], dp[i−1][c − w[i]] + v[i]) when w[i] ≤ c
s10.why: Skip item i, or take it: earn v[i] and use up w[i] of the capacity (only if it fits).

s10.q: Why is O(nW) for knapsack called pseudo-polynomial?
o: W is a numeric value; the input only needs about log W bits to write it
s10.why: The running time grows with the value of W, which can be exponential in the number of bits in the input.

s10.q: In the O(W)-space 1D knapsack, the capacity loop must go:
s10.why: Downward means dp[c − w] still holds the previous item's row, so each item is used at most once. Upward would allow repeats (unbounded knapsack).

s10.q: Min-cost grid path (right/down moves). The first column cell dp[i][0] is computed from:
o: Only the cell on the left
s10.why: There is no column −1, so the only way to arrive is from above.

s10.q: In Python, dp[i-1][j] when i = 0 will:
s10.why: Negative indices wrap around. That is why border cells need separate handling.

s10.q: Which of these is NOT naturally a 2D DP?
o: Climbing stairs with steps of 1 or 2
s10.why: Climbing stairs needs only one index, the step number.

s10.q: Longest common SUBSTRING differs from LCS because:
o: On a mismatch the cell resets to 0, and the answer is the largest cell in the table
s10.why: A substring must be contiguous, so a mismatch breaks the run. The best run can end anywhere.

o: best is the largest value in the whole array
best is the largest value in a[0..i]

b0.q: How many calls to total are made in all by total([2, 7], 0)?
b0.why: i = 0, i = 1 and the base case i = 2. A list of n items makes n + 1 calls.

b0.why: Frames for i = 0, 1, …, n are all waiting when the base case runs, so the recursion uses O(n) space.

o: An infinite loop that runs forever
b0.why: Each call adds a frame. Python caps the depth (about 1,000 by default) and raises RecursionError.

b1.q: What does (n log n) / n² tend to as n grows, and what does it tell you?
o: 0, so n log n = O(n²) but not Θ(n²)
1, so they are Θ of each other
∞, so n log n grows faster

b1.q: How are log₂ n and log₁₀ n related?
o: They differ by a constant factor (about 3.32), so both are Θ(log n)
b1.why: Change of base: log₂ n = log₁₀ n / log₁₀ 2. Constant factors vanish in Θ.

b1.q: In a proof by induction, what does the inductive step show?
o: If P(k) is true then P(k + 1) is true
b1.why: The step is the domino rule: any true case forces the next one. Together with the base case it covers every n.

b1.q: From which n onwards is n² bigger than 100n?
b1.why: n² > 100n exactly when n > 100. The constant 100 delays the crossover but cannot stop it.

b2.q: In a reader–writer partition, what does k mark?
o: The last index of the kept zone
b2.why: a[0..k] holds everything that passed the test. pos is the reader; k only moves when something is kept.

b2.q: pair_sum_sorted uses two pointers from both ends. What does it require?
b2.why: Moving the left pointer up must make the sum bigger, and moving the right pointer down must make it smaller. That is only true when the array is sorted.

b2.q: In three_way, why does mid stay put after swapping with hi?

It should move; that is a bug

b2.q: What is the extra space used by the in-place reverse(a)?
b2.why: Only two index variables, whatever the size of the array.

b3.q: In reverse(head), why save nxt = cur.next first?
o: Because the next line overwrites cur.next, which would lose the rest of the list
b3.why: cur.next = prev destroys the only link to the remaining nodes. Saving it first is what lets the loop continue.

Python requires every function to return
b3.why: If the head is deleted, the caller needs the new head. Returning and re-attaching handles every position the same way, exactly like BST delete.

b4.q: A complete tree has 12 nodes (0-based). What is the index of the last node that has a child?

b4.q: In a 0-based array heap, where are the children of index 4?
b4.why: 2·4 + 1 = 9 and 2·4 + 2 = 10. 8 and 9 would be the 1-based answer.

b4.q: With 1-based numbering (as in CLRS), what is the parent of index 8?
b4.why: 1-based parent is ⌊i/2⌋ = 4. In 0-based numbering the parent of 8 would be (8 − 1) // 2 = 3.

b4.q: What is the height (in edges) of a complete binary tree with 20 nodes?
b4.why: ⌊log₂ 20⌋ = 4: levels hold 1, 2, 4, 8 and then the last 5 nodes.

b4.q: Which priority queue implementation has O(1) insert but O(n) extract-max?
b4.why: Appending is instant, but the maximum must be searched for. A sorted list is the reverse: slow insert, instant extract.

b5.q: How many subsets does a set of 5 items have (including the empty set)?
b5.why: Each item is in or out: 2⁵ = 32.

What is C(6, 2), the number of ways to choose 2 of 6 items?

b5.q: Generating every 3-digit code from 0–9: what does the search tree look like?
b5.why: One level per digit, ten options per digit: 10³ leaves.

b5.q: At about 10⁸ steps per second, up to roughly which n can you list all n! permutations in about a second?
b5.why: 11! ≈ 4 × 10⁷, 12! ≈ 4.8 × 10⁸. Factorials outrun any budget almost immediately.

b10.why: For each x, check whether T − x was seen: O(1) average per lookup.

b10.q: How many ways are there to climb 40 stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time?
b10.why: There are 165,580,141 ways; listing them is pointless when you only need the count, which DP gives in 40 steps.

c1.q: Constraints say n ≤ 10⁵. Which approach is too slow?
o: Sort, then one pass: O(n log n)
A double loop over all pairs: O(n²)
BFS over a graph with n nodes and n edges
c1.why: 10⁵ squared is 10¹⁰ steps, far beyond the roughly 10⁸ simple steps a judge allows per second.

c1.q: The statement says "return the answer modulo 10⁹ + 7". What does that almost always signal?
o: A counting DP whose answer is huge
c1.why: The modulo only matters when the number of ways explodes, which is what counting DPs produce.

c1.q: Why write DFS on a 300 × 300 grid with an explicit stack rather than recursion in Python?
o: Recursion could go 90,000 calls deep, far past Python's default limit of 1,000
Recursion cannot use a visited set
c1.why: Both are O(R · C); the risk is RecursionError (or a crash) on deep inputs.

c1.q: You've spent 15 minutes on Q3 with no new idea and Q4 is unread. Best move?
o: Read Q4; come back to Q3 with fresh eyes
c1.why: Ranking by confidence beats fixed order. Q4 may be easier for you, and stepping away often unblocks Q3.

c1.q: A Codeforces 1600 problem is best described as:
o: The same as a LeetCode-1600 problem
A syllabus technique hidden behind one real observation, about 1900–2100 on LeetCode's scale
A trick question with no algorithm
c1.why: CF ratings run lower than LeetCode's for the same difficulty. Look at the examples: BFS over states, binary search plus BFS, prefix averages.

c1.q: "Distribute the products so that the largest amount any store gets is as small as possible." First idea to try?
o: Binary search on the answer x, checking whether x is enough with a simple count
c1.why: "Minimise the maximum" plus a cheap yes/no check is the binary-search-on-the-answer shape (2064).

c2.q: "Every minute, every infected cell infects its 4 neighbours. How many minutes until all cells are infected?"
o: Multi-source BFS: queue every infected cell first
c2.why: Spreading from many sources at once, counted in levels, is multi-source BFS.

c2.q: "Count land cells from which you cannot walk off the grid."
o: Flood from the border first, then count the land left
c2.why: Removing everything connected to the border leaves exactly the cells that can't escape (1020 Number of Enclaves).

c2.q: Components of sizes 3, 2 and 2 in a 7-node graph. How many pairs of nodes are unreachable from each other?
c2.why: Pairs across components: 3·2 + 3·2 + 2·2 = 16. Equivalently 21 total pairs minus the 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 pairs inside components.

c2.q: Fewest moves through a maze with equal-cost moves. Which tool, and what does it return if the exit is unreachable?
o: DFS, returns the first path found
BFS with a distance array; return −1 if the target is never reached
c2.why: BFS reaches every cell by the fewest moves first; unreached cells keep distance −1.

c2.q: Directed acyclic graph: find the fewest start nodes from which every node is reachable.
o: The node with the highest out-degree
Topological sort, then take the last node
c2.why: Nothing can reach an in-degree-0 node, so each must be a start; in a DAG they reach everything else (1557).

c2.q: Why mark a node visited when it is pushed, not when it is popped?
o: Otherwise the same node can be pushed many times, wasting time and memory
c2.why: Correctness usually survives, but on dense graphs or big grids the duplicates can cause time limits.

c3.q: Frog Jump on heights [10, 15, 0, 20, 5, 25] with jumps of 1 or 2: minimum cost?
c3.why: dp = [0, 5, 10, 10, 15, 15]. The best route is 0 → 1 → 3 → 5, costing 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, the f(5) = 15 from your lecture board.

c3.q: Solving question i forces you to skip the next k questions. Which direction should you fill the DP?
o: Back to front: dp[i] depends on dp[i + 1] and dp[i + k + 1]
c3.why: The future decides what taking i is worth, so compute the later answers first (2140).

c3.q: "Longest subsequence where each element is the previous plus d", n up to 10⁵, values up to 10⁴ in size. Best state?
c3.why: O(n) with a dictionary keyed by value; O(n²) over pairs is too slow at 10⁵ (1218).

c3.q: Counting DP with answer modulo 10⁹ + 7. When should you take the modulo?
o: Never in Python, integers are unbounded
Only when the answer is negative
c3.why: Python would get the right number eventually, but huge integers make every step slower; and in other languages you'd overflow. Mod as you go.

c3.q: You memoize a recursion over n = 10⁵ states with @cache and get RecursionError. Fix?
o: Rewrite it bottom-up as a loop over a table
c3.why: Memoization doesn't reduce depth: the first call still goes 10⁵ frames deep. A table has no recursion.

c3.q: 0/1 subset-sum with a 1D array dp[t]. Which loop direction over t?
o: Upward, so each item can be reused
Downward, so each item is used at most once
c3.why: Upward would let dp[t − x] already include x (bridge 9.5, stop 10).

c4.q: Keep the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals. Sort by:
c4.why: Earliest finish leaves the most room for the rest; the exchange argument proves it (CLRS §16.1).

c4.q: Coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6. Does "largest coin first" give the fewest coins?
o: No: greedy gives 3 coins (4+1+1) but 3+3 uses 2
There is no way to make 6
c4.why: One counterexample is enough to rule out a greedy. Use DP.

c4.q: People must go into boats holding at most two people and a weight limit. Greedy?
o: Pair the two lightest each time
Sort; pair the heaviest with the lightest if they fit, else the heaviest goes alone
Fill each boat with as many as possible
c4.why: The heaviest must go somewhere; the lightest partner is the safest choice (881).

c4.q: Each of 2n people goes to city A or B, exactly n each. Sort by:
c4.why: The difference measures how much each person prefers A; send the n with the smallest difference to A (1029).

c4.q: Which of these is greedy NOT optimal for?
o: Fractional knapsack by value per kg
c4.why: CLRS §16.2: capacity 50, items (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120): greedy gets 160, the best is 220.

o: Depends on the problem: 435 says no, 452 balloons share an arrow at 2
c4.why: Read the statement: it decides whether the comparison is >= or >.

c4.q: Which sort order makes the greedy for “most non-overlapping intervals” correct?
c4.why: The exchange argument swaps the interval that ends first into any optimal schedule without causing a conflict.

c4.q: Greedy by value-per-weight is optimal for…
c4.why: With splitting allowed no capacity is ever stranded; in 0/1 knapsack (60,10), (100,20), (120,30), capacity 50 it gives 160 instead of 220.

c4.q: Coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6: how do greedy and the DP compare?
Task Scheduler (LC 621): what fixes the minimum length?
o: The most frequent task, which forces (top − 1) gaps of width n + 1
c4.why: The busiest task needs top − 1 full frames of n + 1 slots plus a last row; with more tasks than slots the answer is just the task count.

e0.q: Every node has at most one outgoing edge. Starting anywhere and following edges, the walk…
o: can branch, so you need BFS
either stops at a dead end or runs into exactly one cycle and loops there
e0.why: With one way out of each node there is never a choice: a straight tail, then a dead end or a cycle. The ρ shape.

e0.q: a = [1, 2, 0, 2, −1, 4]. How many distinct nodes can you reach from node 3, counting 3?
e0.why: 3 → 2, and 2 sits on the cycle 2 → 0 → 1 → 2 of length 3. Tail 1 + cycle 3 = 4.

e0.q: Subtask 1 has n ≤ 10³. Walking from every node with a seen-set costs about…
o: It never finishes on a cycle
e0.why: Each walk is at most n steps and there are n walks: n² = 10⁶. That alone banks the first subtask.

e0.q: 0/1/2 knapsack with one dp array. Which way does the capacity loop run?
o: Upward, so a copy can build on the previous copy
Downward, so dp[c − w] and dp[c − 2w] still describe the items before this one
Either way gives the same answer
e0.why: Upward reads cells this item already improved, allowing unlimited copies. Downward caps it at the copies you try explicitly.

e0.q: The quickest correct way to turn 0/1/2 knapsack into a problem you already know:
o: Sort by value per weight and take greedily
List every item twice, then run plain 0/1 knapsack
e0.why: Two identical copies are just two items. 2n items, same O(nW) table, nothing new to invent.

e1.q: The final three end-sem problems are CF 1400, 1500 and 1600. What should you guarantee on the 1600?
o: At least a correct brute-force submission for the small subtask
Write the clever idea first and test later
e1.why: A correct slow solution scores the small tests. Full marks on the 1600 are a bonus; zero is avoidable.

e1.q: A subtask says n ≤ 20. Which brute force fits?
o: Nothing: it needs O(n log n)
Running your fast solution and a brute force on many tiny random inputs and comparing
Timing your code on the largest input
e1.why: Tiny random inputs find the edge case you didn’t think of, and the brute force tells you the right answer for it.

e1.q: Reading 2·10⁵ numbers in Python on Codeforces, the safest way is…
o: sys.stdin.buffer.read().split() once, then walk an index
e1.why: One read and one write. Calling input() hundreds of thousands of times can cost a time limit on its own.

e1.q: Fifteen minutes on one problem, no new idea. What now?
o: Submit a brute force if you have one, then move to another problem and come back
e1.why: Bank what you can, then spend time where it buys marks. Coming back fresh often shows the observation.

e2.q: n gifts, each with a price and a joy value. Budget B. Each gift can be bought once. Maximise joy.
e2.why: Items, capacity, maximise value, each once: 0/1 knapsack with a downward capacity loop.

e2.q: Unlimited coins. How many different collections (order ignored) make the amount?
o: Coins in the outer loop, amount upward inside
Amount in the outer loop, coins inside
e2.why: Coins outside means each collection is built in one fixed coin order, so it is counted once (LC 518).

e2.q: Count ordered sequences of steps from {1, 3, 4} that add up to n.
e2.why: Order matters, so every last step is tried at every total: amount outside (LC 377, Climbing Stairs generalised).

e2.q: Split stones into two groups with the smallest possible difference of sums.
o: Subset sum: which totals up to sum/2 are reachable?
e2.why: The best split puts one group as close to half the total as possible: a True/False table over sums (LC 1049).

e2.q: Same 0/1 knapsack code, but the capacity loop runs upward. What does it now solve?
e2.why: Upward lets dp[c − w] already contain this item, so it can be reused without limit. Direction is the whole difference.

e2.q: Sum must be exactly T and you maximise the count of items. How do you start the table?
o: dp[0] = 0 and every other cell −1 (or −∞) for “impossible”
e2.why: Zeros would treat unreachable sums as free. Mark them impossible and skip them in the transition.

e2.q: Memo best(i, c) reads only best(i + 1, ·). To tabulate it, fill i…
o: from n − 1 down to 0 (row n is the base case)
e2.why: A cell must be filled after the cells it reads. Then one row is enough, swept downward over c.

e3.q: Kahn’s algorithm outputs fewer than n vertices. What does that tell you?
o: There is a cycle: those vertices never reach in-degree 0
e3.why: A vertex on a cycle always has an in-edge from the cycle, so it is never queued.

e3.q: Why is BFS wrong for shortest paths with weights?
o: It minimises the number of edges, and a longer route can weigh less
e3.why: Edge 0–1 of weight 4 versus 0–2–1 of weight 1 + 2 = 3: fewer edges, more weight.

e3.q: In heap-based Dijkstra, when is a node’s distance final?
o: When it is popped with d equal to dist[node]
When all its neighbours are pushed
e3.why: A node can be pushed several times as better routes appear. The first pop is the smallest; later pops are stale.

e3.q: You pop (7, u) but dist[u] is already 5. You should…
o: Skip it: it is a stale entry
e3.why: Lazy deletion: old pairs stay in the heap and are ignored when they surface.

e3.q: In the Dijkstra lab graph, what is dist from 0 to 3?
Dijkstra on a graph with one negative edge:
o: Can finalise a node too early and give a wrong distance
e3.why: The “closest popped node is final” argument needs every edge ≥ 0.

e3.q: In Kruskal, union(u, v) returns False for the next cheapest edge. You…
o: Skip it: u and v are already connected, so it would close a cycle
e3.why: An MST has no cycles; union-find answers “already connected?” in near-constant time.

e3.q: Kahn’s algorithm finishes with fewer than n vertices in its output. What does that mean?
o: The graph has a directed cycle
The graph has a negative edge
e3.why: Vertices on or behind a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they are never queued. Disconnected pieces are still peeled.

e3.q: Why can topological DP find a longest path in a DAG when longest path is hard on general graphs?
o: A DAG has no cycles, so each vertex is final before its out-edges are used
Longest path equals shortest path on a DAG
A DAG has at most V edges
e3.why: In topological order every path into a vertex is already counted when you reach it, and no cycle can inflate a path.

e3.q: In Dijkstra, what does a popped heap entry (d, u) with d > dist[u] mean?
o: It is stale: u was already improved, so skip it
e3.why: Heaps cannot lower an existing entry, so improved vertices get a new entry and the old one is skipped when it surfaces.

e3.q: What single assumption does the correctness proof of Dijkstra need?
o: Extending a path never makes it cheaper
e3.why: That is why “minimise the largest edge” (max instead of +) still works, and why negative edges break it.

e3.q: Path With Minimum Effort (LC 1631): what changes from plain Dijkstra?
o: The new cost is max(d, step) instead of d + step
e3.why: The cost of a path is its largest height difference, and max never decreases as the path grows, so Dijkstra still applies.

e3.q: Bellman–Ford on 6 vertices with no negative cycle: how many rounds are always enough?
e3.why: A shortest simple path has at most V − 1 = 5 edges, and round r settles every path of at most r edges.

e3.q: For “at most k stops” (LC 787) you run Bellman–Ford for k + 1 rounds. Why must each round read the OLD distances?
o: Otherwise one round could use several edges and break the limit
e3.why: Reading values updated earlier in the same round lets a path grow by more than one edge per round.

e3.q: Floyd–Warshall: which loop must be outermost?
e3.why: The table must be complete for intermediate vertices 0..k−1 before k is allowed.

e3.q: State the cut property of minimum spanning trees.
o: A lightest edge crossing any cut is in some MST
The heaviest edge overall is never in an MST
Every MST has the same edges
A lightest edge is in every cycle
e3.why: Swap argument: any MST missing that edge can swap it in for another crossing edge without getting heavier.

e3.q: Kruskal’s running time is dominated by…
o: sorting the edges, O(E log E)
e3.why: With union by size and path compression each union-find operation is almost constant.

e3.q: Which MST algorithm suits a complete graph on 2,000 points best?
o: Kruskal with all 2 million edges sorted
e3.why: V² ≈ E, so the heap-free array version has the lowest overhead.

e3.q: In LC 1489, an edge is critical when…
o: removing it makes the MST weight larger (or disconnects)
forcing it in keeps the MST weight
e3.why: It then belongs to every MST. If forcing it in keeps the weight but removing it does not hurt, it is pseudo-critical.

m13.q: Next STRICTLY greater element. Which loop condition is right?
m13.why: Pop everything that x beats, and equal values stay: x is not strictly greater than them. It must be a while loop, because one new value can answer many waiting elements.

m13.q: A monotonic stack handles n elements in…
o: O(n) amortised: each element is pushed once and popped once
O(n log n) because of the stack
O(n) only if the array is sorted
m13.why: The while loop inside the for loop looks quadratic, but every pop removes something pushed earlier: at most n pops in total.

m13.q: Sum of subarray minimums with repeated values. Why is one side strict and the other not?
o: So a subarray with equal minimums is credited to exactly one element
m13.why: If both sides stopped only at strictly smaller values, a subarray with two equal minimums would be counted for both. Making one side stop at equal values assigns it to exactly one.

m13.q: Sliding window maximum with a deque of indices. When do you pop from the front?
o: When the front value is the smallest
When the front index is at most i − k (it left the window)
When the new value is bigger
m13.why: The back is trimmed by value; the front expires by position. The front is always the maximum of the current window.

m13.q: Daily Temperatures for [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]: days to wait for a warmer day?
m13.why: 75 waits 4 days for 76; 71 waits 2 days for 72; 76 and the last 73 never see a warmer day.

x15.q: In tree DP, what order must nodes be processed in?
x15.why: A node’s answer is built from its children’s answers; reversing a parent-first order gives that order without recursion.

x15.q: Maximum Path Sum (LC 124): why can a path that goes UP to the parent use only one child branch?
o: A path cannot split in two directions when it continues upward
x15.why: Only the node where the path bends can use both branches; the value passed upward is the node plus its better branch.

x15.q: When does “binary search the answer” work?
o: When “is x enough?” flips from no to yes exactly once as x grows
When the answer is an integer
When the graph is a tree
x15.why: A monotone yes/no check is the whole requirement; sortedness of the input is irrelevant.

x15.q: Evaluate Division (LC 399) uses a weighted union-find. What does each node store?
o: The ratio of the node to its parent
The edge weight to its neighbour
x15.why: A query is then the ratio of the two nodes to the common root, if they share one.

x15.q: Running median with two heaps: which half goes in the max-heap?
x15.why: The max-heap’s top is the largest of the small half and the min-heap’s top the smallest of the large half; the median sits between them.

x15.q: Why does Word Search II (LC 212) use a trie?
o: One grid walk checks every word at once and cuts paths that match no prefix
x15.why: Without a trie you would search the grid once per word.

x16.q: n ≤ 100,000 and you need the answer within a few seconds in Python. Which cost class is the target?
x16.why: About 10⁷ simple operations per second: n² would be 10¹⁰.

x16.q: n ≤ 20 and “choose any subset”. Which approach fits?
V ≤ 400 and all-pairs shortest paths. Which fits?
x16.why: 400³ = 6.4 · 10⁷, borderline but standard; Bellman–Ford from every source would be V²E.

x16.q: n ≤ 5,000 and a table indexed by two positions. Which cost is allowed?
x16.why: Two-dimensional DP over 5,000 × 5,000 is the usual ceiling.

x16.q: The answer can be up to 10⁹ and you can check any candidate quickly. Which technique?
Which is the correct way to make a 3×3 grid of zeros in Python?
x16.why: The second form makes three names for one row.

x16.q: Why does recursive DFS often fail on a 10⁵-node chain in Python?
o: The default recursion limit is about 1,000 frames
x16.why: Use an explicit stack or a topological peel.
For a max-heap push negated values.

x17.q: Merge sort is stable if, on a tie, the item from…
o: the left half is taken first
the right half is taken first
neither half, the tie is dropped
x17.why: Left items came first in the input, so they must stay first.
The merge needs a buffer for the combined output.

x17.q: Why is appending to a doubling dynamic array O(1) amortised?
o: Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, …, summing to less than 2n over n appends
The array is a linked list
x17.why: Growing by one instead would copy n(n − 1)/2 elements in total.

x17.q: In open addressing, why must a deleted slot become a tombstone, not an empty slot?
o: An empty slot would end searches early and hide keys placed after it
x17.why: Probing stops at the first empty slot.

x17.q: The load factor of a hash table is…
x17.why: Tables resize when it passes a limit such as 0.75 (chaining) or 0.5 (linear probing).
